title: "Orchestration"
description: "The coordination and control of multiple tasks, services, or agents so they work together as an end-to-end system."
term: "Orchestration"
letter: "O"
category: "AI Systems"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Orchestration coordinates the steps in a larger workflow. It determines
what runs, in what order, how components pass results, and what should
happen when a step fails.

## Technical explanation

An orchestrator manages execution across components such as data jobs,
model services, tools, or agents. It may provide dependency handling,
state, retries, timeouts, scheduling, and observability. Workflow
orchestration is distinct from the logic inside each individual task.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

AI applications often combine retrieval, model inference, validation, and
external services. Orchestration makes these steps manageable and
recoverable, but adds complexity that must be controlled with clear
interfaces, limits, and failure handling.

## How it works

The workflow is represented as ordered steps or a graph of dependencies.
The orchestrator starts eligible tasks, records state, passes outputs,
and applies policies for errors and retries. For agent systems, tool
permissions and stopping conditions should be explicit.

## Practical example

A document-processing pipeline could extract text, classify the document,
check required fields, and store the result. If classification fails, the
orchestrator can retry within a limit or route the document for review
without silently treating it as successfully processed.

## Common misconceptions

- Orchestration is not the same as implementing the work performed by each task.
- More components or agents do not necessarily make a workflow more capable or reliable.
- Retrying every failure can duplicate side effects or worsen an outage.
